narrative:
The model determined that you have a 35% chance of representing a bad credit risk. Because this probability exceeded the bank's acceptance threshold, your loan application was denied.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this outcome were the length of the loan you requested, the status of your checking account, and your job type. Your short nine-month loan request was the single biggest reason the model leaned toward approval. Most approved applicants ask for almost twice as long (19 months on average), so a brief duration normally signals lower risk. Unfortunately, this positive push was outweighed by two other important factors.

Your checking account being in negative balance (<0 DM) was the strongest factor pulling the decision toward denial. Only 13% of approved applicants are in this situation, while the majority (59%) have no checking account at all or positive balances. This signaled higher risk to the model. Your job as a manager or self-employed professional also worked against you. Although this is usually viewed positively, in your specific combination of circumstances the model interpreted it as increasing risk compared with the skilled employees who form the bulk of approved borrowers.

Taken together, the negative signals from your account status and occupation proved stronger than the reassuring effect of the short loan duration, leading to the denial.

You should focus on building a positive checking-account balance and, if possible, reapply in a few months with a slightly longer loan term that better matches what successful applicants typically request. This combination of changes would most likely improve your chances. (248 words)
